 Log in If Mets are to land big fish Skubal, Stearns needs to sail uncharted waters
 November 19th, 2026 Anthony DiComo
 Share share-square--:R1qlq: NEW YORK -- One of David Stearns’ most notable remarks at the General Managers’ Meetings last week came in response to a question about his history -- or lack thereof -- of signing starting pitchers to long-term deals. Asked if it’s fair to conclude he has an aversion to such contracts, Stearns answered with a flat: “No.”
 “Every situation is unique,” the Mets' president of baseball operations continued. “It’s been also well publicized even since I’ve been here, we’ve engaged in extremely long-term negotiations for pitchers, and we will do so again. But situation matters. The specific circumstance matters, and we do have to look at every individual pitcher on a case-by-case basis.”

 Whether that means the Mets will ultimately land Tarik Skubal remains to be seen. But it does imply that the Mets, who by all accounts are among the favorites to sign Skubal , should be willing to hand him the largest contract for a pitcher in franchise history.
 It’s a relatively low bar. Despite investing heavily in Juan Soto, Bo Bichette and others, the Mets under Stearns -- and even under Steve Cohen, who owned the team for three offseasons before hiring Stearns as his right-hand man -- have never doled out a pitching contract larger than the five-year, $137.5 million extension Jacob deGrom signed before either of them got here.
 Pre-Stearns, Cohen did demonstrate a willingness to offer large average annual values to pitchers, such as the three-year, $130 million deal Max Scherzer signed before the 2022 season, and the two-year, $86.7 million contract Justin Verlander inked one year later. Those contracts set and tied the Major League AAV record for a pitcher, which stands to this day (not counting Shohei Ohtani, who signed his $700 million megadeal as a two-way player). Both those contracts came under former general manager Billy Eppler.
 Stearns, though? Stearns has never done this type of thing. In Milwaukee, the largest pitching contracts he authorized were pre-arbitration extensions for Aaron Ashby (five years, $20.5 million) and Freddy Peralta (five years, $15.5 million). The most guaranteed money Stearns gave to a pitcher from outside the organization was another $15.5 million over two years for Jhoulys Chacín.
 Here are the largest free-agent contracts in MLB history 
 Since coming to New York, of course, Stearns has taken much bigger swings -- though most of those have come on the offensive side of things. The largest deal he’s given a pitcher was the three-year, $75 million pact Sean Manaea signed after the 2024 season. Clay Holmes got three years and $38 million; Frankie Montas received two years and $34 million. Three of the six richest pitching contracts Stearns has authorized have gone to relievers. Stearns did make Yoshinobu Yamamoto an unsuccessful 12-year, $325 million offer -- the type of deal that falls more in line with what Skubal figures to get. But ultimately, he didn't land the player.
 Skubal represents something entirely different. The Mets have met with the two-time Cy Young Award winner and are reportedly motivated to sign him. Yet to land Skubal, Stearns is going to have to break character and commit massive money to a starting pitcher. He’s going to have to do something he’s never done before.
